MUJAHID:v2p776#2/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p776#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p776#2/r1.claim: Mujahid interprets the sparks as men's stratagems.

MUQATIL:100:1-6/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:100:1-6/r3.speaker: مقاتل
MUQATIL:100:1-6/r3.claim: The horses spark fire from stones with their hooves; the sparks are compared to Abu Habahab’s intermittent flame, which he hid so guests could not benefit.

MUQATIL:100:1-6/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:100:1-6/r4.speaker: مقاتل
MUQATIL:100:1-6/r4.claim: The horses also strike stones and make sparks as they run.

FARRA:v3p284#2/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p284#2/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p284#2/r2.claim: The horses strike sparks with their hooves; the simile is al-Habāḥib's fire.

FARRA:v3p284#2/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p284#2/r3.speaker: الكلبي
FARRA:v3p284#2/r3.claim: Al-Kalbi tells of the extreme miser al-Habāḥib, who lit fires only at night and extinguished them if anyone sought a flame; the horses' sparks are likewise useless.

MAJAZ:v2p307/r2.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p307/r2.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p307/r2.claim: The horses strike fire with their hoof tips.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p390#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p390#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p390#2/r1.claim: Qatada says the horses strike sparks with their hooves.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p390#2/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p390#2/r2.speaker: الكلبي
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p390#2/r2.claim: Al-Kalbi likewise says the horses strike sparks from their hooves.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p536/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p536/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p536/r1.claim: The charging horses strike sparks with their hooves.

TAB-FULL:v24p572/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p572/r6.speaker: ابن عباس وعلي
TAB-FULL:v24p572/r6.claim: In a conversation with Ali, Ibn Abbas first says the oath concerns horses raiding for God's cause and lighting cooking fires at night; Ali counters that Badr had only two horses and identifies the creatures as pilgrims' camels moving from Arafat through Muzdalifa to Mina, and Ibn Abbas recants.

TAB-FULL:v24p576/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r1.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r1.claim: Ikrima says the horses strike and kindle sparks with their hooves.

TAB-FULL:v24p576/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r2.claim: Qatadah identifies the kindle-makers as horses; al-Kalbi says their hooves strike until fire appears.

TAB-FULL:v24p576/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r3.speaker: عطاء
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r3.claim: Ata says the horses kindle fire with their hooves.

TAB-FULL:v24p576/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r4.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r4.claim: Al-Dahhak says the horses strike stones with their hooves to produce fire.

TAB-FULL:v24p576/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r5.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r5.claim: Another interpretation is that the horses kindle war between their riders and the enemy.

TAB-FULL:v24p576/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says the horses raid for God's cause, then return at night so their riders prepare food and kindle a fire.

TAB-FULL:v24p576/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas gives ‘men's scheming’ as another meaning of the kindle-makers.

TAB-FULL:v24p576/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r8.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r8.claim: Mujahid likewise interprets the phrase as men's scheming.

TAB-FULL:v24p576/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r9.speaker: آخرون
TAB-FULL:v24p576/r9.claim: Another interpretation says the kindle-makers are tongues.

TAB-FULL:v24p578/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p578/r1.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v24p578/r1.claim: Ikrima says the kindle-makers are tongues.

TAB-FULL:v24p578/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p578/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v24p578/r2.claim: Ibrahim transmits Ibn Masud's view that camels kindle fire when their hooves scatter stones against one another.

TAB-FULL:v24p578/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p578/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p578/r3.claim: Al-Tabari says the oath can encompass anything that kindles fire: horses striking sparks, people using a fire-stick, tongues kindling speech, men kindling schemes, and horses stirring battle; the wording is general and no proof narrows it.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3457#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3457#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3457#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses sparks as a man's stratagem with a flint that produces a spark.

NAHHAS:v5p277/r10.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p277/r10.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p277/r10.claim: No evidence proves one exclusive referent; the correct interpretation includes anything that kindles, under an understood oath by the Lord of the chargers.

NAHHAS:v5p277/r12.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p277/r12.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p277/r12.claim: Qadḥan is an accusative verbal noun because the sense of the sparkers is 'those who strike sparks.'

NAHHAS:v5p277/r6.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p277/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
NAHHAS:v5p277/r6.claim: One report says people kindle fires so others can see them.

NAHHAS:v5p277/r7.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p277/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
NAHHAS:v5p277/r7.claim: Another report identifies the sparkers as horses.

NAHHAS:v5p277/r9.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p277/r9.speaker: عكرمة
NAHHAS:v5p277/r9.claim: Ikrima identifies the sparkers as tongues.

THALABI:v10p269/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p269/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p269/r2.claim: He first says the chargers are horses raiding in God’s cause, then returning at night to prepare food and kindle a fire.

THALABI:v10p269/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p269/r3.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
THALABI:v10p269/r3.claim: Ali rejects the horse interpretation because at Badr, Islam’s first expedition, the Muslims had only two horses; he says the chargers are camels from Arafat to Muzdalifa and Mina.

THALABI:v10p269/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p269/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p269/r4.claim: After hearing Ali’s argument, Ibn Abbas withdrew his interpretation and adopted Ali’s view; Ibn Masud, Muhammad ibn Umayr, Muhammad ibn Kab, and al-Suddi also held it.

THALABI:v10p269/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p269/r6.speaker: عكرمة وعطاء والضحاك
THALABI:v10p269/r6.claim: They say the horses strike sparks with their hooves as they travel over stones and gravel.

THALABI:v10p269/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p269/r7.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
THALABI:v10p269/r7.claim: They say Arabs call such a fire the fire of Abu Habbab; he was a notoriously stingy pre-Islamic man who extinguished his cooking fire whenever anyone might benefit from it.

THALABI:v10p270/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p270/r1.claim: The phrase means ‘those that strike sparks,’ shifting from the verbal noun to a derived participial form.

THALABI:v10p270/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r2.speaker: قتادة
THALABI:v10p270/r2.claim: He understands the image as horses stirring up war and hostility among their riders.

THALABI:v10p270/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p270/r3.claim: In a report from Ibn Abbas, horses raid for God and return at night to prepare food and kindle their fire.

THALABI:v10p270/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r4.speaker: مجاهد وزيد بن أسلم
THALABI:v10p270/r4.claim: They interpret it as a man’s plotting; Arabic speakers say they will ‘strike sparks’ for someone when plotting against him.

THALABI:v10p270/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r5.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
THALABI:v10p270/r5.claim: He says the sparks refer to men of war.

THALABI:v10p270/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r6.speaker: عكرمة
THALABI:v10p270/r6.claim: He says men’s tongues kindle fires through the force of their speech.

THALABI:v10p270/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r7.speaker: ابن جريج
THALABI:v10p270/r7.claim: A view transmitted by Ibn Jurayj compares successful deeds to a peg succeeding when it catches a spark.

THALABI:v10p270/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p270/r8.speaker: محمد بن كعب
THALABI:v10p270/r8.claim: He identifies the sparks as fires kindled at Jamʿ.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r10.speaker: عكرمة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r10.claim: Ikrimah says it means tongues illuminating proofs, establishing arguments, making truth clear, and exposing falsehood.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r5.speaker: عطاء
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r5.claim: Ata says the horses’ hooves spark fire from the force of their running.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r6.speaker: محمد بن كعب
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r6.claim: Muhammad ibn Kab interprets the phrase as the pilgrims’ fires at Muzdalifah.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas says the phrase means the many fires warriors light to frighten the enemy.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r8.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r8.claim: Qatadah interprets it as stirring up war between the forces and their enemy.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r9.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p323/r9.claim: Mujahid interprets the phrase as men’s stratagems in war.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p327/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p327/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p327/r1.claim: The following Sūrat al-Qāriʿah is Meccan according to all the authorities mentioned.

QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r6.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r6.claim: The horses strike sparks with their hooves against stones while running at night.

QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r7.claim: Alternatively, warriors light a fire after returning from battle.

QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r8.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p442/r8.claim: Another interpretation identifies the sparkers as spearheads.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r1.claim: The passage distinguishes the hard hoof that can spark from a camel's softer, looser foot.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r10.speaker: محمد بن كعب
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r10.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb identifies the sparks with pilgrims lighting their fires at Muzdalifa.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r11.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r11.claim: Another view takes the racing mounts to be camels, with the pilgrim interpretation fitting that identification.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r12.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r12.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r12.claim: Qatada says the horses kindle the fire of enmity between the fighters riding them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r13.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r13.speaker: عكرمة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r13.claim: Ikrima interprets the fire kindlers as tongues that ignite hostility through their speech.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r14.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r14.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r14.claim: Mujahid interprets them as men's thoughts kindling schemes and deceit.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r15.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r15.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r15.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam cites an Arab idiom for stirring up evil, grief, and intrigue against someone.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r16.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r16.speaker: ابن جريج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r16.claim: Ibn Jurayj reads the phrase as those who successfully attain their aims in argument, raiding, or pilgrimage.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r2.speaker: أبو عبيد وأبو الهيثم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r2.claim: Abu Ubayd and Abu al-Haytham cite three Arabic verb forms for kindling or producing fire by striking.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says the horses strike a mountain with their hooves and spark fire like a struck firestick.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r4.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r4.claim: Muqatil says the horses strike sparks from stones, like the fire of al-habhab.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r5.speaker: أبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r5.claim: Abu Ubayda explains that the horses kindle fire with their hoof tips.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r6.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r6.claim: Al-Zajjaj says horses galloping at night strike stones with their hooves and produce sparks.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r7.speaker: عكرمة وعطاء والضحاك
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r7.claim: Ikrima, Ata, and al-Dahhak take qadḥan as an accusative verbal noun, meaning the horses spark as they strike.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r8.claim: On this interpretation, al-muriyat refers to the al-adiyat, the racing horses.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p239#2/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas says the term refers to raiding groups who light fires at night for their needs and food.

WAHIDI-QT:100:2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:100:2/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:100:2/r1.claim: The spark-makers are horses that strike fire with their hooves while galloping at night over stony ground.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:100:1-8/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:100:1-8/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:100:1-8/r2.claim: The horses strike sparks with their hooves over stony ground at night.

JISHUMI:v10p7511/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7511/r1.speaker: الحسن وعكرمة وقتادة
JISHUMI:v10p7511/r1.claim: Al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, and Qatadah say the surah is Meccan; another view says it is Medinan and was revealed around a raid.

JISHUMI:v10p7511/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7511/r11.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7511/r11.claim: Al-mūriyāt is the plural of māriyah and derives from appearing; it describes sparks shown by the horses’ hoof tips.

JISHUMI:v10p7511/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7511/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
JISHUMI:v10p7511/r2.claim: A report promises ten good deeds for reciting the surah for every person who spent the night at Muzdalifah and witnessed Jamʿ.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r1.speaker: عكرمة وعطاء والضحاك ومقاتل والكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r1.claim: They identify the spark-producing runners as horses striking stones with their hooves and making fire.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r14.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r14.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r14.claim: These descriptions are the objects of the oath.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r2.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r2.claim: Qatada says the horses kindle warfare and the fire of enmity between their riders.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r3.speaker: سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says these are horses raiding in God's cause, then returning at night to kindle a fire and prepare food.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r4.speaker: مجاهد وزيد بن أسلم
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r4.claim: Mujahid and Zayd interpret the sparks as men's stratagems in warfare, invoking an Arabic threat meaning that one will kindle a scheme against another.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r5.speaker: محمد بن كعب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p508/r5.claim: Muhammad ibn Kab says the phrase refers to fires coming together.

KASHSHAF:100:2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:100:2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:100:2/r1.claim: The horses strike stones with their hooves and kindle sparks, called the fire of al-ḥabāḥib.

KASHSHAF:100:2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:100:2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:100:2/r2.claim: Qadḥ means striking, while īrāʾ means producing fire; one may strike and kindle or strike without a spark.

KASHSHAF:100:2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:100:2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:100:2/r3.claim: The accusative qadḥan is governed by the same element that governs ḍabḥan in the preceding verse.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p793/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p793/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p793/r4.claim: Al-mūriyāt are horses striking stones with their hooves and drawing the fire called nār al-ḥabāḥib.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p793/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p793/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p793/r5.claim: Qadḥ is striking, and īrāʾ is bringing out fire; qadḥan has the same grammatical construction as ḍabḥan.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p795/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p795/r8.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p795/r8.claim: A report promises ten good deeds for reciting al-ʿĀdiyāt for every person who spent the night at Muzdalifah and witnessed Jamʿ.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p513#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p513#2/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p513#2/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the sparks as those made by horses' hooves striking stones.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p513#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p513#2/r9.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p513#2/r9.claim: Ali and Ibn Masʿud say the camels spark fire as stones they kick strike one another.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r1.claim: Muwriyat qadhan may mean eloquent tongues, a metaphor for arguments that spark and reveal proofs.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r2.claim: Mujahid interprets the phrase as men's cunning.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r3.claim: Qatada says these are horses kindling war, also metaphorically.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r4.speaker: ابن عباس وجماعة من العلماء
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas and others generalize it to anything that strikes fire from flint, a widespread divine benefit linked to 56:71.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r5.speaker: عدي بن زيد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p514/r5.claim: A poem by Adi ibn Zayd describes striking flint and making a fire.

TABRISI:100:1-4/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:100:1-4/r10.speaker: محمد بن كعب
TABRISI:100:1-4/r10.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb says the phrase means fires kindled at Jamʿ.

TABRISI:100:1-4/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:100:1-4/r11.speaker: عكرمة
TABRISI:100:1-4/r11.claim: Another interpretation attributed to ʿIkrimah takes the sparks as men's tongues whose speech kindles fire.

TABRISI:100:1-4/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:100:1-4/r8.speaker: عكرمة
TABRISI:100:1-4/r8.claim: ʿIkrimah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say hooves strike stones to make sparks; Muqātil and Ibn ʿAbbās compare it to flint.

TABRISI:100:1-4/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:100:1-4/r9.speaker: مجاهد
TABRISI:100:1-4/r9.claim: Mujāhid figuratively interprets sparks as men's battle stratagems, using an idiom about kindling a spark against someone.

TABRISI:100:1/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:100:1/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:100:1/r6.claim: Awra is producing fire by striking flint; a weak spark is the fire of al-Ḥabāḥib.

TABRISI:100:1/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:100:1/r7.speaker: النابغة
TABRISI:100:1/r7.claim: Al-Nābighah's line uses ‘fire of al-Ḥabāḥib’ for weak hoof sparks; the name evokes a miser's dim fire.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p206#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p206#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p206#2/r5.claim: In the expedition account, the horses snort through their nostrils, spark with their hooves on stones, attack at dawn, raise dust, and reach the enemy together.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r1.speaker: الجمهور
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r1.claim: Most interpreters say the oath is by horses whose hooves strike sparks from stones as they gallop at night.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r2.claim: Alternatively, the sparks are fires lit by fighters.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r3.speaker: مجاهد وزيد بن أسلم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r3.claim: Alternatively, the sparks are the schemes men make in war.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r4.speaker: القرظي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r4.claim: Alternatively, they are the pilgrims' fires at Muzdalifa.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r5.speaker: عكرمة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r5.claim: Alternatively, they are tongues bringing forward proofs of truth and exposing falsehood.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r6.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p208/r6.claim: A further included statement identifies the third interpretation as the afternoon prayer.

RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r4.claim: On the camel interpretation, the hooves strike stones and spark, or pilgrims riding them light fires at Muzdalifah.

RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r9.speaker: أبي عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v32p60#2/r9.claim: A report attributed to Ubay and raised to the Prophet promises a reward measured by the number who spend a night at Muzdalifah and witness Jamʿ.

RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r1.claim: Irya is bringing out fire and qadh is striking or clashing; the verse has several proposed subjects for the sparks.

RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says horses strike mountains with their hooves and produce sparks like flint.

RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r3.speaker: مقاتل
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r3.claim: Muqatil says the horses' hooves spark against stones like the fire of al-Habhab, a miser who lit fires only after people slept and extinguished them when they woke.

RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r4.claim: A related explanation says iron horseshoes strike stone; the first view is stronger because it makes the horses' own hooves like iron.

RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r5.speaker: قوم
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r5.claim: Others say the horses kindle the fires of war between their owners and enemies, as in the verse about God extinguishing the fire of war.

RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r6.claim: Another view identifies the sparks with fires lit by raiders at night for cooking and other needs; the striking horses are the raiding band.

RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r7.claim: Other metaphorical readings are tongues kindling enmity and men's thoughts igniting deceit; Ibn ʿAbbas is cited for the latter, including fires lit to exaggerate an army's size.

RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r8.speaker: عكرمة
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r8.claim: ʿIkrima says the sparks are made by spearheads.

RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p61#3/r9.claim: A final view reads the phrase as people succeeding in a raid or pilgrimage; it could mean the successful group or its mounts, with a line by Jarir using the idiom of kindling a flint.

RAZI-FULL:v32p62/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p62/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p62/r1.claim: The idiom قدح أورى means a strike that makes sparks, while the same root can metaphorically mean success; literal fire is preferred here.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r1.speaker: عكرمة وعطاء والضحاك
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r1.claim: They interpret al-mūriyāt as horses whose hoofs spark fire; this is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r10.speaker: محمد بن كعب
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r10.claim: Muhammad ibn Kab says the phrase refers to the fires being gathered together.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r11.claim: A metaphorical explanation pictures men’s ideas as fanning the fire of deception and trickery.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r12.speaker: عكرمة
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r12.claim: Ikrimah says the phrase means eloquent tongues reveal proofs, clarify truth, and invalidate falsehood.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r13.speaker: ابن جريج عن بعضهم
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r13.claim: An unnamed report transmitted by Ibn Jurayj interprets the phrase as successfully accomplishing work, like a firestick that catches.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r14.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r14.claim: Al-Qurtubi calls those metaphorical readings figurative and prefers the literal account that horses’ strong gallop makes their hooves spark fire.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r15.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r15.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r15.claim: The Arabs named such sparks nār Abī Ḥabāḥib after a stingy Mudar man who hid a small flame and extinguished it lest others benefit.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r2.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas says the animals raise dust, which the commentator notes conflicts with other reports and fits camels instead.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r3.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r3.claim: A report from Mujahid says Ibn Abbas applied the verses both to battle and to pilgrimage.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r4.claim: Ibn Masud says camels tread pebbles and produce sparks from them.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r5.claim: Qadḥ fundamentally means extracting or bringing something out; the word is used for drawing water from an eye or making fire with a firestick.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r6.claim: Qadḥan has the same grammatical accusative construction as ḍabḥan.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r7.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r7.claim: They also interpret the horses as provoking battle between their riders and the enemy, linked to the verse about God extinguishing fires of war.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r8.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وزيد بن أسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r8.claim: They interpret the phrase as men’s ruses in war; Arabs say I will kindle a fire for you when plotting against someone.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#3/r9.claim: Other explanations are the night fires of raiders preparing food or the many fires warriors light to make an enemy think they are numerous.

QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:100:1-2#4/r1.claim: Al-Nabighah’s poem says swords striking armor kindle the fire of al-Habāḥib, supporting the name for sparks.

BAYDAWI-FULL:100:1-5/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:100:1-5/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:100:1-5/r3.claim: Mūriyāt means those that bring out sparks; īrāʾ is producing fire, as when flint is struck and sparks appear.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#2/r1.claim: The horses kindle sparks as their hooves strike stones; these sparks are called the fire of al-Habāḥib.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#2/r2.claim: Qadḥ means striking, while īrāʾ is bringing out fire; one says a strike kindled fire or failed to kindle it.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p353#2/r3.claim: The accusative qadḥan is governed by the same construction as ḍabḥan in the preceding verse.

QASHANI:100:1-4/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:100:1-4/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:100:1-4/r3.claim: The sparks symbolize conclusions struck from thought and engagement with the Active Intellect, kindled by combining information through reflection.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p526/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p526/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p526/r7.claim: Qadḥ can mean striking or extracting; the eye's removal of impurities and the tools for striking sparks illustrate its range.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p527/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p527/r12.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p527/r12.claim: Mūriyāt describes sparks produced when the horses' hooves strike stones against one another; this spark is called the fire of al-Ḥabāḥib.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r1.speaker: الشاعر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r1.claim: An unnamed poet's line describes the fire of al-Ḥabāḥib sparked by striking stones.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r2.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r2.claim: Qatāda reads the sparking as metaphor: the horses ignite war; Abū Ḥayyān links this image to God's extinguishing war's fires.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r3.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وزيد بن أسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Zayd b. Aslam say the sparking ones are a group plotting against someone, as in the idiom I will kindle against you.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also says the image refers to people lighting night fires for their needs and food.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r5.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās identifies a raiding party whose numerous fires frighten the enemy.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r6.speaker: عكرمة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p528/r6.claim: ʿIkrima says men's tongues kindle a fire through forceful speech, proofs, and arguments that reveal truth and defeat falsehood.

SAMIN-DURR:100:2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:100:2/r1.claim: ‘Qadhan’ may be a verbal noun reinforcing the sparks made by striking, or a circumstantial describing horses striking stones with their hooves to make fire.

SAMIN-DURR:100:2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:2/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:100:2/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says ‘qadhan’ is governed as ‘dabḥan’; he allows an omitted verb, the preceding active participle, or a circumstantial as its governor.

SAMIN-DURR:100:2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:100:2/r3.claim: The fire produced by hooves is called ‘nar al-habahib’; a poem uses that name for the sparks from struck blades.

SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r3.claim: One view takes all the racing, sparking, and raiding descriptions as horses; their descriptions are coordinated in sequence as in a cited poetic example.

SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r4.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r4.claim: A view attributed to the Commander of the Faithful takes the descriptions as camels running from ‘Arafa to Muzdalifa and Mina; a poem by Safiyya bint ‘Abd al-Muttalib supports this interpretation.

SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:100:3/r5.claim: Some interpret ‘al-muriyat’ as a group scheming in war; the idiom ‘I will light you up’ means ‘I will plot against you’.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r1.claim: Ibn Kathir understands the oath as horses running in God's cause: their hooves strike stone and make sparks, and their morning raids raise dust across a battlefield before they enter the enemy ranks.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r4.claim: Ibn Masud interprets the panting runners as camels; Ali also says they are camels.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the runners as horses; when Ali objected that no horses were at Badr, Ibn Abbas clarified that he meant a military detachment.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r6.speaker: علي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p465#2/r6.claim: In Ibn Abbas's account, Ali argues that the runners were camels traveling from Arafat to Muzdalifah and Mina; Ibn Abbas withdraws his earlier view.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466#2/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466#2/r4.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says the Prophet sent horses on an expedition and heard no news for a month; the surah then revealed, and al-Bazzar calls the report very unusual.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r1.claim: Al-Awfi transmits Ibn Abbas's view that the oath refers to horses; many named Successors agree, and Ibn Jarir chooses this view over Ali's camel interpretation.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ata say only a horse or dog makes the panting sound called ضبح; Ibn Abbas imitates it as ah ah.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r3.speaker: أكثر هؤلاء
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r3.claim: Most who interpret the runners as horses say the sparks come from their hooves; Qatadah says they inflame warfare among the riders.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid also interpret the sparks as men's stratagems; others say the phrase describes night fires, tribal fires, or fires lit at Muzdalifah.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r5.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p466/r5.claim: Ibn Jarir prefers that horses make sparks by striking stone with their hooves.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r10.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r10.claim: The horses strike their shoes against stones, especially on rough ground, and thereby cause fire as if forcefully striking flint.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r11.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r11.claim: The horses are credited with the sparks because they cause them, though they do not intend to kindle fire.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p508#2/r9.claim: The following clause names the sparks that galloping produces; the sequencing particle marks the resulting ignition.

DURR-FULL:v8p600/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p600/r2.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v8p600/r2.claim: Their hooves strike stones and kindle sparks.

DURR-FULL:v8p600/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p600/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p600/r8.claim: The horses spark fire with their hoofs as they run over stone.

DURR-FULL:v8p601/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p601/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p601/r11.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the sparks as a man striking his fire-starting stick.

DURR-FULL:v8p601/r18.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p601/r18.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p601/r18.claim: The sparks are a man’s ruse; Arabs say they will strike a spark and kindle it when plotting.

DURR-FULL:v8p602/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r10.speaker: عطية
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r10.claim: Atiyya glosses the sparks as an attack or charge.

DURR-FULL:v8p602/r15.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r15.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r15.claim: Ibn Abbas says the polytheists struck fire while plotting to make themselves seem numerous.

DURR-FULL:v8p602/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r2.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r2.claim: Qatada reads the passage as horses running until panting, striking sparks with their hooves, raiding at dawn, raising dust, entering the people’s gathering; kanud means ungrateful.

DURR-FULL:v8p602/r21.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r21.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r21.claim: Ibn Masud says camel pads strike gravel together, producing sparks.

DURR-FULL:v8p602/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r4.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p602/r4.claim: Mujahid interprets the sparks as a ruse and cites the Arab threat to strike a spark and kindle it.

BURSEVI:v10p383/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p383/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p383/r2.claim: Dabh is the sound of horses' breathing from their mouths and bodies while running, distinct from neighing and the braying sound associated with a pack horse at barley.

BURSEVI:v10p383/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p383/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p383/r3.claim: Grammatically, dabh may be an accusative of the implied verb as a circumstantial phrase, a verbal noun governed by al-‘adiyat, or a circumstantial noun meaning “panting.”

BURSEVI:v10p383/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p383/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p383/r4.claim: The horses strike stony ground with their hooves and shoes, producing sparks; the image uses qadh, striking, for striking stones, and this follows the running whereas panting accompanies it.

BURSEVI:v10p383/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p383/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p383/r5.claim: The forms of qadhan may be analyzed as a verbal noun, a noun attributed to the act, or a circumstantial phrase: “they strike sparks.”

ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r1.claim: Iryāʾ means producing fire and qadhḥ means striking; a strike may ignite or fail to produce fire.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r2.claim: The sparks are from horses striking stones with their hooves, or camels with their feet; such sparks were called the fire of al-Ḥabāḥib after a miser.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r3.claim: قدحا is accusative as a specification transferred from the subject: the animals spark through their striking.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r4.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p215#2/r4.claim: He reads the description metaphorically: the horses ignite the fire of war; the author says this is less apparent.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r15.claim: Qadḥ means striking flint to make sparks; awrā yurī īrāʾan means producing fire by striking a spark.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r16.claim: The clearest interpretation is that horses’ hooves strike stones at speed and spark; the nighttime sparks indicate their power, speed, and night running.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r17.speaker: Bir kısım müfessirîn
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r17.claim: Some exegetes keep the referent as horses but take the sparks figuratively: the riders kindle war between themselves and their enemies, as in 5:64 and the saying that the oven grew hot when battle intensified.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r18.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r18.claim: Another interpretation takes them as raiders lighting fires at night for their needs and food; the phrase is glossed as a group of raiders.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r19.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r19.claim: Those who read al-ʿādiyāt as pilgrims’ camels also explain al-mūriyāt as pilgrims who travel at night from Arafat to Muzdalifa and light a fire at the Sacred Monument.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r20.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r20.claim: Another view identifies the referent as tongues that use harsh, provocative speech to ignite the fire of hostility; qadḥ is then verbal kindling.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r21.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r21.speaker: İbn Abbas
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r21.claim: Ibn Abbas is cited for interpreting them as thoughts that spark deception; the idiom “strike a flint, then make it spark” means to trick someone and stir up trouble or war.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r22.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r22.speaker: İkrime
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r22.claim: Ikrima interprets al-mūriyāt as spears or weapons.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r23.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r23.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r23.claim: Elmalılı extends the image to modern fire-sparking weapons literally and, by extension, fast motorized assault vehicles; a Meccan dating, when Muslims had neither horses nor weapons, would make the future reference especially clear.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r24.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r24.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r24.claim: The distinctive plural forms and successive faʾs suggest an ordered development of attack vehicles through the ages, encompassing motorized raiders as well as horses.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r25.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r25.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r25.claim: A final interpretation reads al-mūriyāt as successful ones who achieve their aims, whether in raiding or pilgrimage; awrā zandahu, literally sparking his flint, means attaining one’s goal.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r26.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r26.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r26.claim: This success reading describes either the successful group or the horsemen; Jarir’s verse about the Azd’s horses and striking flints is cited as evidence for the horsemen reading.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r27.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r27.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r27.claim: The idiom about someone’s flint lighting when struck and satisfying when he gives describes success; the straightforward successful-ones reading is literal, while other figurative readings are less apparent, though weapon sparks are literally possible today.

QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r1.claim: The Meccan surah has eleven verses and moves in rapid, forceful jumps before settling at its ending, like a runner reaching the finish.

QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r2.claim: The opening scene shows charging, panting horses striking sparks, attacking at dawn, raising dust, and suddenly breaking into enemy ranks.

QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r6.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r6.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r6.claim: The rough, rumbling, cracking rhythm suits the noisy dust and forceful disclosure of graves and hearts, as well as the surah’s ingratitude and greed.

QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r7.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r7.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:100:1/r7.claim: The oath’s noisy cavalry scene frames the surah’s moral and resurrection scenes: image and frame mirror one another.

QUTB-ZILAL:100:2/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:100:2/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:100:2/r1.claim: The horses strike stone with their hooves until sparks fly from it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r10.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r10.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r10.claim: Qadh could instead mean drawing broth from a cooking pot into serving bowls for an army or caravan; here it would express purpose.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r7.claim: Al-Muriyat are those that kindle; qadh is striking one surface against another to make a spark, and qadhan is an emphatic verbal noun.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r8.speaker: الشنفرى
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r8.claim: Al-Shanfara's line compares his running to a camel whose hooves make sparks from flint, illustrating extreme speed.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p499/r9.claim: The sparks could be fires lit at night for needs and food, or a metaphor for stirring war, as war is likened to a fire.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p500/r9.claim: The carefully chosen words accommodate both warhorses and pilgrimage camels, a feature of the surah's rhetorical arrangement.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p501/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p501/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p501/r1.claim: The first three descriptions are joined by fa, the usual Arabic pattern for successive adjectives or places; it usually marks sequential occurrence here and in Ibn Ziyaba's verse, but may mark mention order in al-Saffat.

TABATABAI:100:1-5/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:100:1-5/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:100:1-5/r6.claim: Mūriyāt means producing fire and qadh striking; horses' hooves spark on stones.

TABATABAI:100:1-5/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:100:1-5/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:100:1-5/r7.claim: Other readings take the sparks as battle stratagems, kindled fires, or forceful speech; the author calls these weak.

BINTSHATI:v1p104/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p104/r4.speaker: أصحاب التأويل بالخيل
BINTSHATI:v1p104/r4.claim: Horse interpreters argue that the next verse's sparks must come from horseshoes, since camel hooves are too soft to spark, as al-Jurjānī says.

BINTSHATI:v1p104/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p104/r6.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
BINTSHATI:v1p104/r6.claim: Muḥammad b. Kaʿb al-Quraẓī makes the sparkers pilgrims lighting fires at Muzdalifa, requiring an implied word for groups; Ibn al-Qayyim calls this remote and says the sparkers are the runners and raiders.

BINTSHATI:v1p106/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p106/r6.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p106/r6.claim: The root qadḥ occurs in the Qur'an only here; īrāʾ also appears in 56:71 in its basic sense of kindling fire.

BINTSHATI:v1p107/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p107/r1.speaker: أصحاب الإبل
BINTSHATI:v1p107/r1.claim: Camel interpreters cite 56:71 to construe mūriyāt as pilgrims kindling fires at Muzdalifa; Ibn al-Qayyim calls this a remote interpretation and says the sparkers are the runners.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p416/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p416/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p416/r3.claim: Fa-linked clauses are sequential and adjectives apply to the same noun; muwriyāt means producing fire and qadh striking, depicting iron-hoofed horses sparking as they gallop on stony ground.

STUDYQURAN:100:1/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:100:1/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:100:1/r3.claim: Hooves striking rocks cause the sparks.
